data.title: Definitions
sentences: In this Part
(a) “assessment officer” means the court clerk for the judicial centre in which the action is located
(b) “review officer” means an assessment officer who, in the opinion of the clerk of the Court, has for the purpose of reviewing contingency fee or retainer agreements and lawyers’ charges
(i) an acceptable degree in law, and

(ii) sufficient experience in the practice of law, and who is desig- nated as a review officer by [Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.1 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)] Subdivision 1: LAWYERS’ CHARGES

data.title: Payment for lawyer’s services and contents of lawyer’s account
data.text:
(1) Except to the extent that a retainer agreement otherwise provides, a lawyer is entitled to be paid a reasonable amount for the services the lawyer performs for a client considering (a) the nature, importance and urgency of the matter, (b) the client’s circumstances, (c) the trust, estate or fund, if any, out of which the lawyer’s charges are to be paid, (d) the manner in which the services are performed, (e) the skill, work and responsibility involved, and (f) any other factor that is appropriate to consider in the circumstances.
(2) A lawyer may be paid in advance or take security for future lawyer’s charges.
(3) Every lawyer’s account must (a) contain a reasonable statement or description of the services performed, (b) show the fee for the service, and (c) set out separately the details of any disbursements paid or to be paid by the lawyer or any other charges of the lawyer in performing the lawyer’s services.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.2 effective November 1, 2010 Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021]*

data.title: Lawyer acting in representative capacity
data.text:
(1) A lawyer may charge lawyer’s fees for services performed as a lawyer whether or not the lawyer is also acting in the capacity of a guardian, mortgagee, personal representative or trustee.
(2) Despite subrule (1), a lawyer acting as a guardian, mortgagee, personal representative or trustee is not entitled to be paid out of or to charge to a trust, an estate, a fund, mortgaged property or a mortgage loan for which the lawyer performs lawyer’s services unless (a) the Court orders the amount paid or charged, (b) every person interested in the trust, estate, fund, mortgaged property or mortgage loan is legally competent and agrees to the payment or the charge, or (c) the lawyer’s charges have been reviewed and certified by a review officer.
(3) This rule does not apply to client funds held by a lawyer in the lawyer’s trust account.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.3 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*

data.title: Charging order for payment of lawyer’s charges
data.text:
(1) On application by a lawyer, the Court may declare property specified in its order, including property that may be subsequently recovered in an action, to be subject to a charge as security for payment of the lawyer’s charges.
(2) The order referred to in subrule (1) may only be made if (a) the lawyer establishes to the Court’s satisfaction that the lawyer’s charges will not be or are unlikely to be paid unless the order is made, and (b) the property to be the subject of the charge is associated with (i) the action conducted by the lawyer on the client’s behalf, and (ii) the lawyer’s services result in the recovery or preservation of the client’s property.
(3) An order may also be made under this rule if (a) a lawyer who performed services for a client in the recovery or preservation of property under a contingency fee agreement ceases to be the client’s lawyer before the event or contingency occurs and those services are likely to, or might, result in the recovery or preservation of the client’s property, and (b) the requirements of subrule (2)(a) and (b) are met.
(4) On application, the Court may make any other order necessary to obtain the amount required to pay the lawyer’s charges from the property subject to the charge.
(5) An order must not be made under this rule if in all the circumstances the Court considers that to make the order would be unfair.
(6) Nothing defeats or affects a charge on property imposed under this rule unless the property is disposed of to a bona fide purchaser for value without notice of the charge.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.4 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*

commentary.text:
On it’s face, a charging order under rule 10.4 securing payment of legal fees may only be made, pursuant to subrule (2), if two requirements are satisfied. First, the lawyer must establish that the fees are unlikely to be paid without the order. Second, the property to be charged must be associated with the lawyer’s work and that work must result in recovery or preservation of the property. “The purpose of r 10.4(2) would be best met by permitting the 10.4(2)(a) requirement to be established at the time of bringing the application for a charging order, or within a reasonable time subsequently.” Paragon Capital Corp. v. Starke Dominion Ltd., [2020] A.J. No. 618, 2020 ABCA 216 at para. 51 (Alta. C.A.).
The requirement in rule 10.4(5) that a charging order must not be made if doing so “would be unfair” is not the same as considering “whether unfairness would arise from refusing the order, rather than from granting it”, although on the facts that may be a reasonable inference. Paragon Capital Corp. v. Starke Dominion Ltd., [2020] A.J. No. 618, 2020 ABCA 216 at paras. 53-54 (Alta. C.A.).
The court may refuse to exercise equitable interference on behalf of a lawyer if the lawyer was delayed excessively in bringing forward a claim for the lien. If a lawyer’s delay has been excessive and the rights of others have suffered due to the delay, the court can choose to not interfere. M. (D.S.) v. S. (K.L.), [2021] A.J. No. 1749, 2021 ABQB 1024 at para. 25 (Alta. Q.B.).
Priority of Charging Orders – The determination of the priority of a charging order granted under this rule to other registered interests requires a contextual analysis, it is not always that they take such priority. Paragon Capital Corp. v. Starke Dominion Ltd., [2020] A.J. No. 618, 2020 ABCA 216 (Alta. C.A.); see also , [2021] A.J. No. 1758, 2021 ABQB 988 at para. 13 (Alta. Q.B.). Robertson LLP v. Pasco RETAINER GREEMENTS A

data.title: Retainer agreements
data.text:
(1) A lawyer may make an agreement with a client about the amount and manner of payment of the whole or any part of past or future lawyer’s charges for services performed by the lawyer.
(2) The amount a lawyer is to be paid may be determined in any appropriate way, including (a) a gross sum, (b) commission, (3) The amount payable may be at the same or at a greater or lesser rate than the rate to which the lawyer would be entitled under rule 10.2 [Payment for lawyer’s services and contents of lawyer’s account] if no retainer agreement were entered into.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.5 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*

commentary.text:
A lawyer seeking to collect on a contingency fee who has not complied with rule 10.7 cannot obtain assistance from rule 10.5.22 The Rules are clear on this.
There is no duty to discuss assessment (absent a contingency agreement) when making a retainer. However, like rule 10.7(7) (on contingency agreements) it might be appropriate for the Rules of Court Committee to recommend to the Lieutenant Governor in Council a rule that provides a future requirement that each account of a lawyer to a client contain a notice to the effect that a right to review is available, with some time limitations — including that it be brought within two years of the date of the account, unless extended by other factual or legal considerations.
Principles of interpreting a retainer agreement: Samson Cree Nation v. O’Reilly & Associés, [2014] A.J. No. 904, 2014 ABCA 268 at paras. 53, 81-82, 110, 165-169 (Alta. C.A.).
• Certainty has value for both the client and the lawyer.
• If there is any doubt on how to interpret the words in a contract, courts should look to what is practical and workable to achieve the aim of the parties.
• Where a contract has several clauses or parts or terms, they are to be interpreted harmoniously to achieve the overall objective.
• A claim for a remedial order in the context of a dispute between a lawyer and client is made within the meaning of the , when the appointment Limitations Act for assessment is taken out. Any account pre-dating two years prior to this appointment is statute barred.
• The word “interim” has two meanings, and thus correspondence describing accounts as interim settles nothing. The first meaning is “between two times or ‘before then’”. This meaning has “nothing to do with finality versus tentative- ness”. The second meaning is that the thing is subject to change. Samson Cree Nation v. O’Reilly & Associés, [2014] A.J. No. 904, 2014 ABCA 268 at para. 110 (Alta. C.A.). This was reiterated in Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co. Inc. v. Bennett • The court must hold the lawyer and the client to promises made in a retainer

data.title: Void provisions
data.text:
(1) In a retainer agreement or otherwise, a provision is void if the provision (a) purports to relieve a lawyer from liability for negligence or any other liability to which the lawyer might be subject as a lawyer, or (b) purports to provide that an action, application or proceeding cannot be abandoned, discontinued or settled without a lawyer’s consent.
(2) Despite any agreement to the contrary, a client may change the client’s lawyer or act on the client’s own behalf before a retainer agreement ends.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.6 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*

Subdivision 3: CONTINGENCY FEE AGREEMENTS

data.title: Contingency fee agreement requirements
data.text:
(1) A contingency fee agreement must (a) be in writing, and (b) be signed by the lawyer and the lawyer’s client or by their authorized agents.
(2) To be enforceable, a contingency fee agreement must contain the following particulars in precise and understandable terms:
(a) the name and address of each client;
(b) the name and address of the lawyer;
(c) a statement of the nature of the claim;
(d) a statement of the event or contingency on which the lawyer’s fees are to be paid to the lawyer;
(e) a statement about (i) the manner in which the contingency fee is to be calculated, provided that no fee, calculated as a percentage or otherwise, may be payable on disbursements or other charges recovered, (ii) the maximum fee payable, or the maximum rate calculated, detailing the disbursements and other charges that are included (3) The contingency fee agreement must be witnessed by a person who sees the client sign the agreement, and that person must then swear an affidavit of execution.
(4) The client must be served with a copy of the signed contingency fee agreement within  Steinke v. Hajduk Gibbs LLP, [2014] A.J. No. 62, 2014 ABQB 34 at para. 50 (Alta. Q.B.). days after the date on which the agreement is signed, and an affidavit of service to that effect must be executed by the person who served the agreement.
(5) A client may terminate a contingency fee agreement without incurring any liability for the lawyer’s fees under the agreement if the client, within Rath & Co. v. Sweetgrass First Nation, [2013] A.J. No. 268, 2013 ABQB 165 at para. 77 (Alta. Q.B.), revd but not on principles of law, [2014] A.J. No. 1392, 2014 ABCA 426 (Alta. C.A.), leave to appeal refused [2015] S.C.C.A. No. 67 (S.C.C.). days after service on the client of the copy of the contingency fee agreement, gives written notice of the termination to the lawyer, but the client is liable to reimburse the lawyer for reasonable disbursements incurred by the lawyer.
(6) If a contingency fee agreement provides that a lawyer is entitled to an amount from a costs award, the lawyer is not entitled to receive from the costs award any higher percentage of the judgment or settlement than the lawyer is entitled to receive under the contingency fee agreement.
(7) Every account rendered under a contingency fee agreement must contain a statement that at the client’s request a review officer may determine both the reasonableness of the account and the reasonableness of the contingency fee agreement.
(8) An account that does not contain the statement required by subrule (7) is of no effect unless the Court (a) is satisfied (i) that the omission of the statement was inadvertent, and (ii) the client has not been misled or prejudiced, and (b) the Court waives the requirement for the statement.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.7 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021); Alta.*

data.title: Lawyer’s non-compliance with contingency fee agreement
data.text:
If a lawyer does not comply with rule 10.7(1) to (4), (6) and (7) [Contingency fee agreement requirements], the lawyer is, on successful accomplishment or disposition of the subject-matter of the contingency fee agreement, entitled only to lawyer’s charges determined in accordance with rule 10.2 [Payment for lawyer’s services and contents of lawyer’s account] as if no contingency fee agreement had been entered into.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.8 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*

data.title: Reasonableness of retainer agreements and charges subject to review
data.text:
The reasonableness of a retainer agreement and the reasonableness of a lawyer’s charges are subject to review by a review officer in accordance with these rules, despite any agreement to the contrary.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.9 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. May 15, 2021)]*

data.title: Time limitation on reviewing retainer agreements and charges
data.text:

(2) A lawyer’s charges may not be reviewed, whether at the request of the lawyer or the client, if one year has passed after the date on which the account was sent to the client.

sentences: The purposes of rule 10.10 are as follows: • give the client a fair opportunity to challenge a retainer agreement and/or accounts
• put lawyers on notice that a client has concerns in case they have an ongoing relationship

• encourage clients to voice concerns close to the date they arise, which allows both parties to retain records and make notes relevant to the concerns, and helps prevent the difficulty of assessing complaints years after difficulties may have occurred
• allow lawyers to anticipate uncollectible receivables, or to know that collected accounts may have to be returned, within a reasonable period of time
• allow lawyers to have finality of accounts. Rath and Co.
